analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all federal funding for the agency that enforces workers' union rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in committee with just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill would cut off every dollar of federal funding for the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB), the federal agency that enforces laws protecting workers who want to form unions and penalizes employers that fire or retaliate against them [S2] [S3]. Without funding, the agency could not run union elections or investigate employers accused of illegal retaliation. The bill was introduced in May 2015 and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never took it up [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, particularly those facing union organizing drives or enforcement actions, would benefit. The NLRB is the federal referee for union-related workplace disputes; without it, companies accused of illegally firing pro-union workers or interfering in union elections would face no federal enforcement of those rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers opposing union organizing and enforcement

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit any appropriation of funds for the National Labor Relations Board, cutting off the agency's entire budget.

The NLRB conducts union representation elections and investigates and prosecutes employers for unfair labor practices such as firing workers for union activity; ending its funding would end those functions.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would pay. Private-sector employees rely on the NLRB to run union elections and to investigate employers that fire, demote, or retaliate against workers for organizing. With no enforcement agency, those protections would exist on paper only.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers seeking union rights and enforcement

drawbacks.text: Cutting all NLRB funding would leave the federal government with no agency to enforce workplace union protections, investigate illegal retaliation, or run union elections.

The bill's one-sentence approach offers no replacement process for resolving unfair labor practice cases or conducting representation elections, which employers themselves use to validate organizing outcomes.

Supporters' implicit argument is that the NLRB is an agency whose rulings they consider overreaching; the bill removes the referee entirely rather than reforming its decisions, leaving both compliant and non-compliant employers without an enforcement mechanism.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's single provision would zero out the main federal enforcement body for private-sector workers' organizing rights. Whatever policy dispute motivated the sponsor, cutting the agency's entire budget rather than legislating specific reforms means every protected activity the law guarantees would become unenforceable, and the heaviest burden would fall on workers who cannot individually afford to litigate retaliation cases.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and later to a subcommittee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 15, 2015, with Rep. Matt Salmon (R-AZ) as sponsor and one cosponsor, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
In November 2015 the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action was taken.
The bill never advanced beyond committee in the 114th Congress (2015-2017) and never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers' union protections stayed intact, because the bill's sole mechanism, defunding the NLRB, never advanced. Employers that had backed similar defunding efforts gained nothing from this bill, though the NLRB also avoided the policy challenge its critics wanted.

for.name: Rep. Matt Salmon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit any appropriation of funds for the NLRB.

for.name: One House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional support it drew.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it received no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Republicans, and no Democrats supported it; the bill drew no action in the Republican-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Employers facing union organizing or NLRB enforcement
industries.note: The bill would defund the agency that polices employer retaliation against union activity, removing the main check on such practices and lowering the risk of organizing succeeding.

Unions depend on NLRB-supervised elections and NLRB prosecution of employers that fire organizers; without the agency, forming and defending unions would become far harder for their members and potential members.
